title: 3-Read Friday #42: Independent Tasks, Learning Words, and Homework
author: Craig Barton
summary: This issue of 3-Read Friday pairs classroom-level implementation problems with a cognitive-science aside from Barton's own family life. He opens with Peter Foster's diagnosis of what goes wrong in the first moments of independent work, a scenario Barton says he sees constantly when observing lessons. He then turns personal, describing a conversation with his young son that led him to Michael Pershan's post on the overlap between learning maths and learning language, framing it through his own fascination with watching his child's mathematical understanding develop. He closes with Jo Castelino on homework, prompted by a school Barton visited where completion rates fell to 17 percent among older, lower-set students, a data point he uses to underline how intractable the homework problem can be precisely because so much of it happens outside teachers' view.
points: Barton uses a real observed classroom pattern (slow starts, stuck students, rising noise) to frame why Foster's independent-task diagnosis resonated with him.
He shares a concrete data point from his own consulting work: a school with only 17 percent homework completion in Years 7-11, worse still among lower sets.
He frames homework as structurally hard to fix because, by definition, it happens outside teachers' direct control.
He draws a personal, anecdotal link between his three-year-old son's early number talk and Pershan's argument about language and maths learning overlapping.
quotes: The teacher sets the students off on independent work, and almost immediately, a number of problems occur: some students are slow to start, some immediately get stuck, the noise level in the room creeps up, and so on.
Pete drills down into the specific nature of some of these issues and provides some concrete strategies for dealing with them.
Michael describes a fascinating conversation between him and his three-year-old son, revealing an important distinction between maths and language learning.
I recently visited a school with a 17% completion rate for online homework across Years 7 to 11.
Many schools have a homework problem, and it is tricky to solve because - by definition - homework is work done (or not done!) outside of teachers' control.
Jo outlines some of the key issues here, and teases what is sure to be a cracking new book on the subject.
